steps.title: Santiago's valley
steps.body: The Maipo Valley surrounds Chile's capital, Santiago, in the north of the Central Valley. It stretches from the Andes in the east toward the Coastal Range in the west, following the Maipo river. It's small by Chilean standards, about 11,000 hectares, but historically the most important for fine red wine.
steps.highlight: Around Santiago, along the Maipo river

steps.title: Mediterranean with Andean breezes
steps.body: Maipo has a warm, dry Mediterranean climate: hot summers, mild winters, rain mostly in winter. Cool air flows down from the Andes at night, giving a big day and night swing. Irrigation from the Maipo river, fed by Andean snowmelt, is essential. Like all Chile, it's free of phylloxera, so vines are ungrafted.

steps.prompt: What cools the Maipo Valley at night?
options: Cold air flowing down from the Andes
steps.explanation: Mountain air drains into the valley.

steps.title: History
steps.body: In the mid-19th century, wealthy Chilean families, inspired by Bordeaux, brought French grapes, mostly before phylloxera reached Europe's vineyards. They founded estates near Santiago, like Cousiño Macul, 1856, Santa Rita, 1880, and Concha y Toro, 1883, now Chile's largest wine company. Chilean Cabernet's reputation began here.
steps.highlight: Cousiño Macul, Santa Rita, Concha y Toro

steps.prompt: Chile's vineyards are free of phylloxera.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its natural barriers have kept it out, so vines are ungrafted.

points: Maipo surrounds Santiago, along the Maipo river
Warm days and cold Andean nights shape its wines
